3a9c2dfea7: Build00:20–00:55 Part 1: Pitch and the staff
6cccdf9eb1: The staff: the higher the position, the higher the note
19b32bb4b3: Also called the G clef: its curl centres on the second line, and that line is G (Sol).
53221b3ff0: Notes beyond the five lines get short lines added above or below; middle C, for example, sits on the first ledger line below.
9ce1f8f7dd: Guitar music is written an octave up: middle C on the page actually sounds an octave lower.

7029006af4: Whole and half steps on the guitar
9a01d39b0d: On the guitar, each fret is a half step and two frets are a whole step. So Mi→Fa and Si→Do are only one fret apart, and all other neighbouring notes are two frets apart.
f669cb6e57: Cut a bar in half, then in half again
a9e7d80ac3: Western music mostly divides in twos: each level down, the note is half as long and there are twice as many. From eighth notes down, a beam joins the notes in the same beat.
3ce50a9bd0: A small dot to the right of a note adds half its length: dotted quarter = 1 + ½ = 1.5 beats; dotted half = 3 beats.
a60c70033d: On a rest your hand stops and the sound is cut, while you keep counting in your head. Lots of songs stop suddenly at a key moment, and it sounds especially cool.

4d6d60cb13: Close-up photos of left-hand fretting: on the left, fingers naturally curved, pressing the string with the fingertip just behind the fret; on the right, the pad of the thumb supporting on the back of the neck
2839016019:
Fingertip close to the fret
Fingers curved, leaving room for the next stringThumb supports from behind
Pad resting lightly on the middle of the neck
fc4e95313b: ① Close to the fret: press toward the right side of the fret space; it takes the least effort and buzzes least
c356f892fd: ② Fingertips upright: use the area between tip and pad, with fingers close to 90 degrees to the fretboard so they clear the next string
48a9d04dac: ③ Thumb behind: on the middle line at the back of the neck, squeezing with the fingers like a clip, supporting from behind
61a87b8691: ④ Just enough pressure: stop once the note sounds clean; pressing too hard tires you out and pushes the pitch sharp
9ab38832c7: Finger crawl 1-2-3-4: one finger per fret
95e41d2ea5: Index on fret 5, middle on fret 6, ring on fret 7, little finger on fret 8. The right hand alternates "down, up" with the pick. When you press the next fret, keep the earlier fingers on the string.
5ee04392eb: Finger crawl 1-3-2-4: make each finger independent
9ed98d61f6: Left-hand control and stretch, right-hand speed and accuracy.
0f1797a59a: Only add 4 BPM after two steady rounds in a row. The original handbook's 100 BPM is the final goal; start slow.
f0b21fee0a: Once it's comfortable, crawl from fret 1, where the frets are widest and the finger stretch does the most good.
8c18d87761: Each group lines up; each person takes one string, and the next person carries on with the next string
608e9010b0: Metronome at 70 BPM; if the whole group stays steady across all six strings, 2 points
0546ea4bac: If someone stops or slips, pick up again from that person, 1 point
dfd1bad265: Round two goes up to 80 BPM; go for the group's top speed
a17c9b5f16: Fifth-fret tuning: use the next string as your reference
d7395fdfd1: The two notes in each pair should match
0afbdef466: String 6 fret 5 = open string 5 AString 5 fret 5 = open string 4 DString 4 fret 5 = open string 3 GString 3 fret 4 = open string 2 BString 2 fret 5 = open string 1 E
56837b4e4a: Why string 3 uses fret 4: strings 3 and 2 are a major third apart, while all other neighbouring strings are a perfect fourth apart. The tuning diagram from Chapter 1 comes in handy here.
